sections.title: Alphabet and Phonics
sections.explanation: English has 26 letters. Each letter has a capital and a small form. Phonics means learning the sounds letters make so you can blend them into words. Vowels are a, e, i, o, u; the other letters are consonants. Practise sounding out words on the school bus signboard and on tiffin labels.
points: A–Z capitals and a–z small letters
Vowels: a, e, i, o, u
Other letters are consonants
Blend sounds: c-a-t → cat
Listen for beginning, middle and end sounds

sections.title: Sight Words and Vocabulary
sections.explanation: Sight words appear again and again in stories, so we learn to read them quickly without sounding out every letter. Words like the, said, come and friend help you read classroom charts and storybooks. Growing vocabulary means noticing new words at the market, in festivals and in school notices.
points: Common words: the, a, and, is, to, you, I, said
School words: here, come, look, play, friend, school
Read sight words in short sentences
Make a personal word wall at home
Use new words when you speak

sections.title: Singular and Plural
sections.explanation: Singular means one. Plural means more than one. Many naming words add -s to become plural, like cat → cats. Some add -es after sounds like s, x, ch or sh, as in bus → buses. A few special words change in other ways, like child → children. Count the mangoes in a basket to practise!
points: Singular = one; plural = more than one
Often add -s: book → books
Add -es after s, x, ch, sh: box → boxes
Some words change specially: child → children, foot → feet
Match verbs: one cat runs; two cats run

sections.title: Opposites (Antonyms)
sections.explanation: Opposites are words with nearly opposite meanings, like hot and cold or big and small. Learning opposites helps you describe weather in the monsoon and feelings after a cricket match. When you know one word, its opposite gives you a second useful word for speaking and writing.
points: big / small, tall / short, hot / cold
happy / sad, open / close, day / night
in / out, up / down, fast / slow
Opposites help describe clearly
Use opposites in short oral sentences

sections.title: This, That, These, Those
sections.explanation: We use this and these for things near us. We use that and those for things farther away. This and that talk about one thing; these and those talk about more than one. Point to a nearby tiffin box and say this, then point to a far blackboard and say that.
points: this = one thing near you
that = one thing far from you
these = many things near you
those = many things far from you
Point while you speak to make meaning clear

sections.title: Rhyming Words
sections.explanation: Rhyming words end with the same sound, like cat and hat or sun and fun. Rhymes make poems, songs and festival chants easy to remember. Clap the ending sound and listen carefully. You can invent funny rhymes about monsoon rain and school bags!
points: Rhymes share the same ending sound
cat–hat–mat; sun–fun–run
ball–tall–call; day–play–say
Rhymes help reading and spelling
Not all similar spellings rhyme; listen to sound

sections.title: Nouns (Naming Words)
sections.explanation: A noun names a person, place, animal or thing. Common nouns name ordinary things like school or ball. Proper nouns name special ones and begin with a capital letter, like India, Monday or Numair. Spot nouns on festival invitation cards and classroom name charts.
points: Person: teacher, Numair
Place: Delhi, school, park
Animal: cat, parrot
Thing: ball, book, tiffin
Proper nouns start with a capital letter

sections.title: Pronouns
sections.explanation: Pronouns stand in for naming words so we do not keep repeating names. I, you, he, she, it, we and they are common pronouns. If Numair has a bat, we can say He has a bat. Matching the pronoun to the person or thing keeps sentences smooth.
points: I, you, he, she, it, we, they
he for a boy; she for a girl; it for a thing/animal sometimes
we for a group that includes you
they for more than one person or thing
Pronouns avoid repeating the same noun

sections.title: Verbs: Simple Present & Present Continuous
sections.explanation: Verbs are doing or being words. Simple present talks about habits: I go to school. Present continuous talks about actions happening now: I am going to school. Watch for -ing and helping words am, is, are. Describe what you do every morning and what you are doing right now in class.
points: Verbs show action or being: run, eat, is, are
Simple present: habits — She reads every day
Present continuous: now — She is reading
Use am / is / are with -ing forms
Match the verb to the subject

sections.title: Adjectives (Describing Words)
sections.explanation: Adjectives describe nouns. They tell size, colour, shape, taste or feeling — a red apple, a tall tree, a happy child. Good adjectives make festival stories and picture talks more interesting. Try adding one describing word before school, monsoon or cricket.
points: Adjectives describe people, places and things
Colour: red, green, blue
Size: big, small, long, short
Feelings: happy, sad, brave
Place the adjective near the noun it describes

sections.title: Articles & Punctuation
sections.explanation: A and an are small words before naming words. Use a before consonant sounds and an before vowel sounds: a bat, an apple. The points to a special one. Sentences start with a capital letter and often end with a full stop. Questions end with a question mark; excitement can use an exclamation mark.
points: a before consonant sounds; an before vowel sounds
the for a particular person or thing
Start sentences with a capital letter
Full stop (.) ends most sentences
Question mark (?) for questions; (!) for strong feeling

sections.title: Prepositions (Place Words)
sections.explanation: Prepositions show place or position: in, on, under, behind, between, near. They tell where something is. The cat is under the table. The ball is in the basket. Use these words when you describe your classroom, the school bus or Rangoli on the floor.
points: in, on, under, over
behind, in front of, between, near
Prepositions answer where?
Use real classroom objects to practise
One clear preposition is better than guessing

sections.title: Writing About Myself & School
sections.explanation: Writing a few clear sentences about yourself builds confidence. Start with your name, age and class. Add one line about your school, friends or favourite game like cricket. Use capitals, full stops and simple present tense. Keep ideas in order so a reader can follow easily.
points: Say who you are in the first sentence
Add age, class and school name
Write one hobby or favourite subject
Use I with verbs like am, like, play, go
Check capitals and full stops

sections.title: Picture Composition & Reading
sections.explanation: Picture composition means looking carefully at a picture and writing or saying sentences about it. Notice who is there, where they are and what they are doing. For reading, find the main idea and important details. Festival scenes, market stalls and monsoon parks make lively picture talks.
points: Observe people, places and actions in the picture
Write 3–5 short sentences in order
Use naming words, doing words and describing words
In passages, find who / what / where
Answer in complete sentences when asked

examples.answer: The children are flying a kite in the park. (sample)
